summary: An Oblivious Pseudorandom Function is a two-party protocol where a server holds a key and a client gives an input, and the client learns the output without learning the key. The server learns neither input nor output. This document also defines verifiable variants, so clients can check the key used. It comes from the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: An oblivious pseudorandom function lets a client ask a server to compute a value with the server's secret key, without the server learning what was asked and without the client learning the key. The client hides the question by multiplying it by a random number, the server cannot undo that without the key, and the client removes the random number at the end. The verifiable variants add a proof so the client can also check that the server used the key it expected.

questions: oblivious pseudorandom function how does it work
subtitle: Two-party protocols to compute with a server's key without revealing the input to the server or the key to the client.

tldr.problem: A server holds a secret key for a pseudorandom function, and a client wants that function evaluated on a private input. Standard approaches either reveal the input to the server or require the server to hand out its key.
tldr.mechanism: The client blinds its input before sending it, the server evaluates the function with its key without learning the input, and the client unblinds the result. The verifiable variants add a discrete logarithm equivalence proof so the client can check which key was used.
tldr.outcome: Three variants address different needs: OPRF for plain obliviousness, VOPRF with a proof the key was the expected one, and POPRF with a public input known to both sides. These support password-protected secret sharing, password authentication and privacy-preserving tokens.

today: RFC 9497 is an Informational RFC published in December 2023 by the Crypto Forum Research Group, and it has not been obsoleted. It is the specification behind the oblivious PRF used in password-authenticated key exchange and privacy-preserving token systems.

sections.title: Three Ways to Compute Without Revealing
sections.content:
A Pseudorandom Function (PRF) F(k, x) is an efficiently computable function taking a private key k and a value x as input. The function is pseudorandom if the keyed function K of the input is indistinguishable from a randomly sampled function acting on the same domain and range.

An Oblivious PRF (OPRF) is a two-party protocol between a server and a client. The server holds a PRF key k and the client holds an input x. The protocol lets both parties cooperate in computing F(k, x), so that the client learns F(k, x) without learning anything about k, and the server does not learn anything about x or about F(k, x).

A Verifiable OPRF is an OPRF in which the server also proves to the client that F(k, x) was produced by the key k corresponding to the server's public key, which the client knows. A Partially Oblivious PRF is a variant of a VOPRF in which the client and server interact in computing F(k, x, y), with a server-provided key k, a client-provided input x and a public input y, and the client receives proof that the value was computed using the key matching the public key the client knows. A POPRF with a fixed input y is functionally equivalent to a VOPRF.

OPRFs have a variety of applications, including password-protected secret sharing schemes, privacy-preserving password stores, and password-authenticated key exchange. Verifiable OPRFs are necessary in some applications, such as Privacy Pass, and have also been used for password-protected secret sharing schemes.

This document specifies OPRF, VOPRF and POPRF protocols built upon prime-order groups. It describes each protocol variant along with application considerations and their security properties. It represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group; it is not an IETF product and not a standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudorandom function is a keyed function whose output looks random. The oblivious version lets a client use the server's key without the server seeing the input and without the client seeing the key. The verifiable version adds a proof that the server used the key the client already knows, which matters when the client has to trust a particular server rather than any server.

sections.title: Preliminaries: The Group and the Proof
sections.content:
The protocols have two primary dependencies. The group is a prime-order group providing the operations described in the document, and the hash is a cryptographic hash function whose output length is Nh bytes. Section 4 of the document specifies ciphersuites as combinations of group and hash.

The group is assumed to be additive and of prime order, denoted Group. In such a group any element other than the identity can generate the other elements, and one element is usually fixed as the generator. The fundamental operation is addition with identity element I; for any elements A and B, A plus B is also a member of the group, and for any A there exists an element minus A such that A plus minus A is the identity. Scalar multiplication by r is repeated addition, written r times A, and for any element A, p times A is the identity. Scalar multiplication of the generator is written ScalarMultGen. Given two elements A and B, the discrete logarithm problem is to find an integer k such that B is k times A. The scalars correspond to the prime field of order p, the integers from 0 to p minus one. The document uses the types Element and Scalar for these two sets.

The group interface includes Order, which outputs the order of the group, Identity, Generator, RandomScalar to choose at random a nonzero element of the field, and ScalarInverse. Two hashing functions are defined: HashToGroup(x) maps bytes deterministically to a group element and must make it computationally difficult to reverse the mapping, and HashToScalar(x) maps bytes deterministically to a field element. Both may take a domain separation tag, and their security properties are described in RFC 9380. There are also serialization functions: SerializeElement and SerializeScalar map values to canonical fixed-length byte arrays, and their deserialization counterparts fail if the input is not a valid canonical representation, raising a DeserializeError if the deserialization fails or if the element is the identity.

For some elliptic curves, those of RFC 7748 for instance, which require accounting for cofactors, the ciphersuite sections describe the steps needed to ensure the resulting group is of prime order.

A proof of knowledge allows a prover to convince a verifier that some statement is true. A proof the prover can generate without interacting with the verifier is noninteractive. A proof where the verifier learns nothing other than whether the statement is true is zero-knowledge. The document describes a noninteractive zero-knowledge proof for discrete logarithm equivalence, used in the construction of VOPRF and POPRF. A DLEQ proof demonstrates that two pairs of group elements have the same discrete logarithm without revealing the discrete logarithm.

The proof resembles the Chaum-Pedersen proof, which was shown to be zero-knowledge and becomes noninteractive after applying the Fiat-Shamir transform. A later result showed a proof system for batching DLEQ proofs with constant-size proofs regardless of the number of inputs, and the system presented follows that construction with two modifications: the transcript used to generate the seed includes more context information, and the individual challenge for each element is derived from a seed-prefixed hash-to-scalar invocation rather than being sampled from a seeded pseudorandom number generator.

Generating a proof takes a scalar k, an element A, an element B, and two non-empty lists of elements C and D of length m, and produces a proof that k times A is B and that k times C[i] is D[i] for each i. The output is a pair of scalars. The function accepts lists of inputs so that applications can produce a single constant-sized proof for m inputs rather than m separate proofs. It computes composite elements M and Z from the inputs, draws a random scalar r, forms t2 as r times A and t3 as r times M, serialises the relevant elements, and builds a challenge transcript from the serialised B, M, Z, t2 and t3 together with the string Challenge. The challenge is the hash of that transcript mapped to a scalar, and the second component of the proof is r minus the challenge times k.

Verifying takes the same inputs plus the proof and returns a boolean. It recomputes the composites, forms t2 as s times A plus c times B and t3 as s times M plus c times Z, rebuilds the same transcript, and checks that the challenge derived from it equals the challenge in the proof. Because the composites are built by hashing the inputs with a seed derived from B and the context string, a proof generated for one set of inputs can be verified against lists of inputs whenever the proof was generated as a batched proof with the same inputs.
sections.plainLanguage:
Everything is done with additions and multiplications in a prime-order group, and a hash turns a password or token into a point in that group. The interface is small: find the group's order and generator, hash bytes to a point, hash bytes to a number, and serialize or parse either one, refusing anything that is not the canonical form.

The verifiable variants need the server to prove that the key it used is the one whose public key the client already holds. The proof says that two pairs of points share the same secret exponent, without revealing that exponent. One proof can cover many evaluations at once, and its size does not grow with the number of evaluations.

sections.title: The Online Protocol
sections.content:
Each of the three variants involves two messages between the client and the server, but they differ in their security properties. Each protocol has an offline setup phase and an online phase.

In the OPRF mode, the client blinds its input: it draws a random scalar blind, maps the input into the group with HashToGroup, fails with an InvalidInputError if the result is the identity element, and forms the blinded element as blind times the input element. The client keeps the blind and sends the blinded element to the server. The server multiplies the blinded element by its private key skS and sends the result back. The client then unblinds: it computes the inverse of the blind and multiplies the evaluated element by it, serialises that element, and hashes it together with the input and the string Finalize to produce the output.

An entity that knows both the private key and the input can compute the same result directly, using the Evaluate function, which hashes the input into the group, multiplies by the key and hashes the serialised result with the input.

In the VOPRF mode, the client additionally receives a proof that the server used skS. The server proves, with a zero-knowledge proof, that the key it used is the same key that produced the public key pkS that the client holds as input; the proof does not reveal the private key. In BlindEvaluate the server multiplies the blinded element by skS and generates a proof relating the generator and pkS to the blinded and evaluated elements. The client verifies the proof and, if verification fails, raises a VerifyError; otherwise it unblinds and hashes as before. Larger lists let the server evaluate several elements at once and produce a single batched proof, and the client can then verify several inputs at once.

The POPRF mode extends VOPRF so that the client and server can additionally provide a public input used in computing the PRF, so the output is F of skS, the input and the info value. The client's blinding step also binds the public info value, producing an additional tweaked key used later in the protocol; the function can fail for private inputs that map to the identity element and for certain public inputs that, if not detected then, would cause the server's evaluation to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: Two messages do the work. The client multiplies its input by a random number and sends that; the server multiplies by its key and sends the result; the client divides out its random number and hashes the answer. Because the server only ever sees the blinded value, it cannot tell what was asked, and because the client never sees the key, it cannot use the server's function on its own.

sections.title: Modes, Ciphersuites and Setup
sections.content:
Each of the three protocol variants is identified with a one-byte value: OPRF is 0x00, VOPRF is 0x01 and POPRF is 0x02. Each variant is also instantiated with a ciphersuite, identified by an ASCII string identifier. The mode and the ciphersuite identifier are combined into a context string used throughout the protocol, built as the prefix OPRFV1, the one-byte mode value, a hyphen and the identifier.

A ciphersuite wraps the functionality the protocol needs, and must be available to both client and server, with agreement on the instantiation assumed throughout. It contains a group, a prime-order group exposing the operations of Section 2.1 with the generator defined in the corresponding reference, and which also specifies HashToGroup, HashToScalar and the serialization functions; the domain separation tag for HashToGroup is constructed in accordance with the recommendations of RFC 9380. It also contains a hash function whose output length is Nh bytes. The document gives an initial set of ciphersuites: ristretto255 with SHA-512, decaf448 with SHAKE-256, P-256 with SHA-256, P-384 with SHA-384, and P-521 with SHA-512. Future documents can specify additional ciphersuites as needed. The document warns that applications should take caution in using the P-256 and ristretto255 ciphersuites, for the reason given in the security section.

In the offline setup phase, the server generates a fresh random key pair. There are two ways to do so: the GenerateKeyPair function, and a deterministic variant. The deterministic variant derives the key from a seed and a counter: it derives a scalar from the input concatenated with a counter byte, using the domain separation tag DeriveKeyPair concatenated with the context string, incrementing the counter until the result is nonzero, and computing the public key by multiplying the generator by that scalar. The setup functions for each mode build the context string from the mode and the identifier and return the key material and the context.
sections.plainLanguage: The mode and the ciphersuite name are folded into a context string that is mixed into every hash, so results from one use of the protocol cannot be replayed into another. The server's key can be generated at random or derived deterministically from a seed, which lets a server keep several keys for different purposes and rebuild them after a restart.

sections.title: What Applications Have to Handle
sections.content:
Inputs, expressed as private or public input values, MUST be smaller than 2^16 minus 1 bytes in length. Applications that need longer inputs can use a cryptographic hash function to map them to a fixed-length input within the bounds, noting that some hash functions have input length restrictions of their own, though these are often large enough not to be a concern in practice, and SHA-256 for instance has an input limit of 2^61 bytes. The length restriction exists because private and public input values are length-prefixed with two bytes before use throughout the protocol.

Although the interface of the protocol functions allows some inputs and outputs to be group elements and scalars, implementations can operate over those values internally and expose only an interface over an application-specific message format.

Several operations can fail, and the errors are listed so that applications can handle them deliberately. A VerifyError means proof verification failed, in the verifiable variants. A DeserializeError means a group element or scalar could not be deserialized. An InputValidationError means validation of byte array inputs failed. Two more are rare in practice: an InvalidInputError when blinding produces an invalid output element, and an InverseError when a tweaked private key has no multiplicative inverse. The document notes that the errors are a guide for implementors and are not an exhaustive list of what an implementation might emit; an implementation might run out of memory and return a corresponding error.

On the public input of the POPRF variant, public input allows clients and servers to cryptographically bind additional data to the output. A POPRF with fixed public input is functionally equivalent to a VOPRF, but the two variants make different underlying security assumptions. The public input is known to both parties at the start of the protocol, and it is RECOMMENDED that it be constructed with some type of higher-level domain separation to avoid cross-protocol attacks, for example by ensuring the public input uses a unique, prefix-free encoding. Implementations of the POPRF may choose not to let applications control the info value in cases where it is fixed or otherwise not useful, in which case the resulting protocol is functionally equivalent to the VOPRF.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need care. Inputs have a length limit, because they are length-prefixed inside the protocol, so anything longer has to be hashed first. And the public input in the POPRF variant is bound into the result, so it has to be built so that one protocol's value cannot be reused in another.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limits
sections.content:
The security properties of an OPRF protocol with functionality y equals F of k and x include those of a standard PRF. Pseudorandomness means that for a random sampling of k, the output on any input x is indistinguishable from uniformly sampling any element in the range of the function. A consequence of showing that a function is pseudorandom is that it is necessarily nonmalleable: a new evaluation cannot be computed from an existing one. Unconditional input secrecy means the server learns nothing about the client input even with unbounded computation. In practice this is the property that even if the server later learns the input, it cannot link any particular evaluation to it, which is also known as unlinkability. Beyond client input secrecy, in the OPRF protocol the server learns nothing about the output and the client learns nothing about the server's private key.

For VOPRF and POPRF there is an additional property, verifiability: the client must only complete the protocol if it can assert that the output it computes is correct with respect to the private key held by the server. In practice this requires the server to commit to the key before the protocol runs, and the client to verify that the key used matches that commitment, which may be referred to as a public key. The POPRF variant adds partial obliviousness, which requires that the protocol can be performed on the client's private and public input, with the server learning nothing about the private input or the output and the client nothing about the private key. This becomes useful for key management operations such as rotation of the server's keys.

The OPRF and VOPRF variants are based on the JKK construction, with two distinguishing properties: this document does not use session identifiers to differentiate instances of the protocol, and it supports batching so that multiple evaluations happen at once while only one proof object is constructed. Their pseudorandomness and input secrecy, and verifiability, rest on the One-More Gap Computational Diffie-Hellman assumption. That analysis was for one instance of the protocol and without batching; there is currently no security analysis available for this document's VOPRF in a setting with multiple server keys or with batching. The POPRF construction is based on 3HashSDHI, and its properties rest on the One-More Gap Strong Diffie-Hellman Inversion assumption, which reduces to the discrete logarithm assumption in the algebraic group model for some number of BlindEvaluate queries.

There is one limit worth stating plainly. These protocol variants instantiate an oracle for constructing static Diffie-Hellman samples, which are meant to recover bits of the server's private key. The best known attacks reduce the security of the group instantiation by log2(Q) / 2 bits, where Q is the number of BlindEvaluate calls made by the attacker. Choosing a group with a 128-bit security level therefore instantiates an OPRF with a reduced security level of 128 minus log2(Q) / 2 bits. Such attacks are only possible for applications where the adversary can query the OPRF directly, and applications can mitigate by rate-limiting client queries to BlindEvaluate or by rotating private keys; where no such oracle is available, the loss does not apply. In most cases it would take an informed and persistent attacker to spend a great deal to reduce security to much below 100 bits. Applications that admit the oracle and cannot tolerate less than 128 bits of discrete logarithm security are RECOMMENDED to choose groups targeting a higher level, such as decaf448, P-384 or P-521.

Two further points apply. Applications SHOULD construct the protocol input to provide domain separation, so that a system with several OPRF applications distinguishes its client inputs and the results stay separate. And all operations that use secret data MUST run in constant time, including all prime-order group operations and the proof-specific operations such as GenerateProof and BlindEvaluate, so that no information leaks during execution.
sections.plainLanguage: The client learns the answer and nothing about the key; the server learns nothing about the question. The verifiable variants add a check that the right key was used. One caveat is spelled out: giving an attacker repeated access to the protocol lets it try to recover the server's key, so the effective security drops as it makes more calls, and applications that cannot limit that should pick a larger group.

viz.caption: THE SECURITY PROPERTIES THE VARIANTS PROVIDE

items.title: Pseudorandomness
items.text: The output is indistinguishable from a random value, so a new evaluation cannot be derived from an old one.

items.title: Unconditional input secrecy
items.text: The server learns nothing about the input even with unlimited computing power, and cannot link an evaluation to an input it later learns.

items.title: Key secrecy
items.text: The client learns nothing about the server's private key.

items.title: Verifiability
items.text: In VOPRF and POPRF, the client finishes only if it can check that the key used matches the public key it already held.

items.title: Partial obliviousness
items.text: In POPRF, the private and public inputs are both used, which helps with tasks such as rotating the server's keys.
